name: Language in different media
intro: How language and devices vary between news, social media, advertising, spoken media and formal writing, how to compare them, and differences between varieties of English.
sammendrag:
## Language changes with the medium

We adapt our language to where we communicate. A news article, a text message, an advert and a podcast all use English – but in very different ways. Comparing them shows how **language** and **devices** (techniques) are chosen to fit the **medium**, **purpose** and **audience**.

## News

News articles aim to inform. They often follow the **inverted pyramid**: the most important information comes first (who, what, when, where, why), then the details. **Headlines** are short and catchy and often leave out small words: “PM resigns after scandal”. **Tabloid** newspapers use more dramatic language, puns and emotional words than **broadsheet** newspapers.

## Social media

Language on social media is short, informal and quick:

- **abbreviations** like tbh, idk and imo
- **emojis**, **hashtags** and **memes**
- **slang** that changes fast
- posts written to get **engagement**: likes, comments and shares

Many influencers mix personal stories with marketing.

## Advertising

Adverts want to **sell**. Common devices are

- **imperatives** (commands): “Buy now!”, “Just try it!”
- **positive adjectives**: new, amazing, fresh, best
- **slogans**: short, memorable phrases
- **alliteration**, rhymes and wordplay
- **direct address**: talking to “you”
- promises about how the product will make you feel

## Spoken media

**Podcasts**, radio and online videos use spoken language with **fillers** (um, like, you know), questions to the audience and a conversational tone. Speeches often use **rhetorical questions**, repetition and the **rule of three**: listing three things for rhythm and effect.

## Formal writing

Reports, essays and applications use **formal** language: complete sentences, precise vocabulary, no slang and few contractions. The tone is neutral and objective.

## Comparing texts

When you compare language in different media, look at

- **register**: formal or informal?
- **sentence length** and structure
- **word choice**: neutral, emotional, technical or slang?
- **devices**: imperatives, rhetorical questions, repetition, alliteration
- **visual elements**: pictures, emojis and layout
- **purpose and audience**: Why is the language like this?

## English around the world

English also varies between countries. **British English** (colour, lorry, flat) and **American English** (color, truck, apartment) differ in spelling and vocabulary. Other varieties, such as Australian, Indian and Nigerian English, add their own words and expressions. Choose one variety and use it consistently in your writing.

flashcards.def: The channel used to communicate, like a newspaper, podcast or social media.
A language technique used for a particular effect.
A news structure with the most important information first.
The short title of a news article.
A newspaper with dramatic, emotional language and big headlines.
A newspaper with more serious, neutral language.
A word or phrase with # that groups posts on social media.
Likes, comments and shares on social media.
A short, memorable phrase used in advertising.
Talking directly to the audience as “you”.
Words like um, like and you know in spoken language.
A question asked for effect, not to get an answer.
Listing three things for rhythm and effect.
Varieties with different spelling and words, like colour/color and flat/apartment.

quiz.text: What is the inverted pyramid in news writing?
options: A way to end an article
Putting the most important information first
quiz.explain: Readers get the key facts even if they stop early.

quiz.text: Which of these is an imperative?
quiz.explain: Imperatives tell the reader to do something.

options: A short, memorable phrase used in advertising
quiz.explain: Good slogans are easy to remember.

quiz.text: Which is typical of language on social media?
quiz.explain: Social media language is short and informal.

options: A question asked for effect, not to get an answer
quiz.explain: “Who doesn't love summer?” is an example.

quiz.text: Which headline is typical of a tabloid newspaper?

options: Words like um, like and you know in speech
quiz.explain: Fillers make spoken language sound natural.

quiz.text: Which features are typical of formal writing?
options: Complete sentences, precise vocabulary and no slang
quiz.explain: Formal writing is used in reports, essays and applications.

quiz.text: Why do adverts often use the word “you”?
options: To speak directly to the audience and involve them
To avoid saying the product's name
quiz.explain: Direct address makes the reader feel personally involved.

ekstra.text: News headlines often leave out small words.
ekstra.explain: “PM resigns after scandal” leaves out words like “the” and “has”.

ekstra.text: Adverts usually use neutral, objective language.
ekstra.explain: Adverts use positive and emotional language to sell.

ekstra.text: British and American English can have different spelling.
The same kind of language is used in all media.
ekstra.explain: Language is adapted to each medium, purpose and audience.

ekstra.text: What is the rule of three?
options: Listing three things for rhythm and effect

ekstra.text: Which word describes how formal or informal language is?
ekstra.explain: We choose register based on the situation.

ekstra.text: What is engagement on social media?
ekstra.explain: Many posts are written to get as much engagement as possible.

skriv.text: A news article and a podcast discuss the same event. Compare one language feature you would expect in the news article with one you would expect in the podcast. Explain how each feature fits its medium.
skriv.fasit: A news article may put the most important information first, while a podcast may use fillers and a conversational tone. The article is written, but the podcast uses spoken language.
kriterier: Gjør en relevant sammenligning mellom språk i en nyhetsartikkel og en podcast.
Knytter forskjellen til at det ene mediet er skriftlig og det andre muntlig.

skriv.text: Compare the language of a tabloid newspaper with the language of a broadsheet newspaper.
skriv.fasit: A tabloid often uses dramatic, emotional language, while a broadsheet usually uses more serious and neutral language.
kriterier: Beskriver tabloidens dramatiske eller følelsesladde språk.
Setter dette opp mot broadsheetens mer seriøse eller nøytrale språk.

skriv.text: A student adds #SchoolGarden to a social media post. Explain what the hashtag does and how it can help people find related posts.
skriv.fasit: A hashtag is a word or phrase with # that groups social media posts. People can use it to find other posts about the school garden.
kriterier: Forklarer at en hashtag grupperer innlegg om samme tema.
Forklarer at den kan gjøre relaterte innlegg lettere å finne.

skriv.text: An advert for a snack says, “Crispy crackers create a cheerful crunch.” Identify one language device in the sentence and explain how it helps the advert.
skriv.fasit: The repeated “cr” sound is alliteration. It gives the phrase a catchy rhythm that may help people remember it.
kriterier: Identifiserer allitterasjon eller positivt ladede adjektiv.
Forklarer hvordan språkbruken kan gjøre reklamen mer fengende eller minneverdig.

skriv.text: In a speech about a cleaner park, a speaker asks, “Who wouldn’t want a cleaner park?” Explain what kind of question this is and what effect the speaker may want it to have.
skriv.fasit: It is a rhetorical question because the speaker is not expecting an answer. It can make the audience think about or agree with the idea of a cleaner park.
kriterier: Forklarer at spørsmålet ikke først og fremst er ment å få et svar.
Beskriver en relevant effekt på publikum, for eksempel å få dem til å tenke eller støtte poenget.

skriv.text: A speaker says, “We need courage, patience and teamwork.” Name the speech device used in the list and explain its effect.
skriv.fasit: The speaker uses the rule of three by listing three things. This can give the words rhythm and make the point more effective.
kriterier: Identifiserer at listen består av tre ledd, altså regelen om tre.
Forklarer at dette kan skape rytme eller gi poenget større effekt.

skriv.text: A student writes, “The colour of my new apartment is blue.” Rewrite the sentence consistently in British English or American English, and name the variety you chose.
skriv.fasit: In British English: “The colour of my new flat is blue.” I chose British English and used its spelling and vocabulary consistently.
kriterier: Velger britisk eller amerikansk engelsk og oppgir hvilken variant.
Bruker både stavemåte og ordvalg som passer til den valgte varianten.

skriv.text: An influencer tells a personal story in a social media post and then recommends a product. Explain how the post combines personal content with marketing.
skriv.fasit: The personal story is part of the post, while the product recommendation promotes something to the audience. The influencer combines personal content with marketing.
kriterier: Forklarer at innlegget både deler en personlig historie og promoterer et produkt.
Knytter produktanbefalingen til markedsføring eller salg.
